content: Severe and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in patients receiving penicillin therapy. These reactions are more likely in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. Patients with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity may also experience severe reactions when treated with cephalosporins. Before initiating therapy with Bicillin C-R, a thorough inquiry into the patient’s history of hypersensitivity to penicillins, cephalosporins, or other allergens is essential. If an allergic reaction occurs, Bicillin C-R should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. Severe anaphylactic reactions require emergency treatment with epinephrine, along with oxygen, intravenous steroids, and airway management, including intubation, as clinically indicated. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including Bicillin C-R. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibacterial therapy alters the normal flora of the colon, leading to overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile can cause increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even if it occurs up to two months after the last dose. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be instituted as clinically indicated. Bicillin C-R must not be injected into or near an artery or nerve, as this may result in permanent neurological damage. Inadvertent intravascular administration, including direct intra-arterial injection or injection near arteries, has resulted in severe neurovascular damage, such as transverse myelitis with permanent paralysis, gangrene requiring amputation, and necrosis or sloughing at the injection site. These severe effects have been reported following injections into the buttock, thigh, and deltoid areas, particularly in infants and small children. Other complications of suspected intravascular administration include immediate pallor, mottling, or cyanosis of the extremity distal and proximal to the injection site, followed by bleb formation and severe edema requiring fasciotomy. Bicillin C-R must not be administered intravenously or mixed with other intravenous solutions, as inadvertent intravenous administration of penicillin G benzathine has been associated with cardiorespiratory arrest and death. Repeated intramuscular injections of penicillin preparations into the anterolateral thigh have been associated with quadriceps femoris fibrosis and atrophy. Prescribing Bicillin C-R in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Penicillins should be used cautiously in individuals with significant allergies or asthma. Care must be taken to avoid intravenous or intra-arterial administration or injection near major peripheral nerves or blood vessels, as these may cause neurovascular damage. A small percentage of patients may be sensitive to procaine. Sensitivity can be identified by the development of erythema, wheal, flare, or eruption following administration of a 1–2% procaine solution. Procaine sensitivity should be treated with standard methods, including barbiturates, and procaine penicillin preparations should not be used. Antihistamines may be beneficial in managing procaine reactions. Antibiotic use may result in the overgrowth of nonsusceptible organisms, necessitating constant observation of the patient. If new infections due to bacteria or fungi occur during therapy, the drug should be discontinued, and appropriate measures should be taken. Allergic reactions require discontinuation of penicillins unless the condition being treated is life-threatening and only amenable to penicillin therapy. During prolonged therapy with penicillin, particularly at high doses, periodic evaluation of renal and hematopoietic systems is recommended. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, patients may develop watery and bloody stools, with or without stomach cramps and fever, even up to two months after completing antibiotic therapy. If this occurs, patients should contact their physician immediately. Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including Bicillin C-R, should only be used to treat bacterial infections and not viral infections (e.g., the common cold). Patients should be advised to complete the full course of therapy as directed, even if they feel better early in the treatment course. Skipping doses or not completing therapy may reduce the effectiveness of treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance. In streptococcal infections, therapy must be sufficient to eradicate the organism to prevent sequelae of streptococcal disease. Cultures should be taken after treatment to confirm eradication of streptococci. Penicillin G has been classified as Pregnancy Category B. Reproduction studies in animals have shown no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus. Human experience with penicillins during pregnancy has not shown adverse effects on the fetus, but adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women are lacking. Therefore, penicillin G should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. Soluble penicillin G is excreted in breast milk, and caution should be exercised when administering penicillin G benzathine or penicillin G procaine to nursing women. No long-term animal studies have been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic, mutagenic, or fertility-impairing potential of these drugs. Clinical studies of penicillin G benzathine and penicillin G procaine have not included sufficient numbers of elderly patients to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. However, other clinical experience has not identified differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. Dose selection for elderly patients should be cautious, starting at the lower end of the dosing range, reflecting the greater frequency of decreased hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, and the presence of concomitant disease or other drug therapy. This drug is substantially excreted by the kidneys, and the risk of toxic reactions may be greater in patients with impaired renal function. Monitoring renal function may be useful in elderly patients.
